readerTitle: Your new drink gets one chance on the shelf. Where should it start?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (중견 식품회사의 신제품 음료 팀, 유통 채널 결정) · 적용 레슨으로 MKT-08-01, MKT-08-03 개념을 사용
insight: 새 음료의 첫 판매처는 가장 큰 시장이 아니다. 매장당 판매 속도를 증명할 수 있는 가장 좁은 곳에서 시작하고, 그 증거로 다음 단계를 연다.
misconception: 한 번에 최대한 많은 매장에 깔아야 판매가 커진다. 큰 유통 기회가 오면 무조건 잡아야 한다.

sources.text: 모든 인물, 회사, 매장 수는 설명용 가상 예시
소매 유통의 일반적 관행 (입점비, 매장당 판매 속도에 따른 상품 정리)

factChecks.note: 소매업체가 매장당 판매 속도로 신제품을 평가하고 잘 안 팔리는 상품을 정리한다는 내용은 일반적 관행으로만 서술했습니다. 특정 유통사의 기준, 기간, 비율은 쓰지 않았습니다. 게시 전 표현이 과장되지 않았는지 확인하세요.
입점비(listing fee)는 나라와 유통사마다 관행이 다릅니다. 카드에서는 가상 제안의 조건으로만 언급했습니다.
매장 수(40곳, 600곳, 30곳)는 모두 설명용 가상 수치이며 계산에 쓰이지 않습니다.

cards.title: Your new drink gets one chance on the shelf.
body: Maya leads a small new-products team inside a mid-size food company. Her team has made a sparkling ginger drink that tasters love.
The head of sales has a plan: put it in every supermarket the company already supplies, all at once, by summer. It sounds bold. It may be the fastest way to kill the drink.

image.label: One new drink bottle on a long, crowded supermarket shelf
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 수백 개의 음료가 빽빽한 긴 마트 진열대 한가운데 새 생강 탄산음료 한 병이 작게 놓여 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음. 병 라벨은 단순한 생강 그림만.

cards.title: Who should get the drink first?
body: Maya has a modest launch budget. She can focus it on one group of customers to start.

options.text: Everyone who buys soft drinks. It's the biggest market
options.feedback: Huge reach, but most soft-drink buyers have no reason to switch. The budget spreads thin and the signal gets lost in the noise.

options.text: People in one city who already pay for ginger shots and kombucha at cafés and health stores
options.feedback: This is **who to sell to first**: people who already want this kind of drink and are easy to reach in a few places. Their reorders become proof.

options.text: Young adults across the country, through social media ads
options.feedback: A clearer target than everyone, but scattered. Ads can reach them, yet most can't find the drink in a store near them.

cards.eyebrow: Concept at work · Who to sell to first
cards.title: Start where the need is already strong.
body: The first customers should be the ones who need the product most and are easiest to reach. Cafe regulars buying ginger shots already spend money on this kind of drink. You don't have to convince them the category exists.
They also do something a national audience can't: they come back. A café that reorders every week tells Maya more than a million ad views.

cards.title: Stores judge speed, not total sales.
body: A retail buyer watches how fast a product sells **per store**, not how much it sells overall. Shelf space is limited, so slow items are often dropped to make room.
Spread the same early demand across hundreds of stores and every store looks slow. Once a drink is dropped, getting it back in is much harder than getting in the first time.

image.label: Same sales spread thin across many stores versus concentrated in a few
image.brief: 두 장면 비교. 왼쪽: 매장 아이콘 수십 개에 판매 막대가 아주 짧게 하나씩. 오른쪽: 매장 아이콘 몇 개에 판매 막대가 높게. 두 쪽의 전체 판매량은 같다는 것을 작은 합계 표시로 보여줌. 실제 유통사 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A big chain offers 600 stores.
body: A distributor calls. A national supermarket chain will list the drink in 600 stores next month, if Maya's company pays a listing fee.
Meanwhile, about 40 cafés and health stores in one city are ready to stock it now. What should she do?

options.text: Take the 600 stores. Chances like this don't come often
options.feedback: Fast reach, but there's no proof yet that supermarket shoppers will buy. Sales per store will likely look weak, and the chain may drop it.

options.text: Start with the 40 cafés and stores, then take the reorder numbers to a regional chain
options.feedback: This is **launch sequencing**: each stage earns the next. Strong numbers from 40 places make a far better pitch than hope across 600.

options.text: Take the 600 stores and pay for heavy in-store discounts to keep sales up
options.feedback: Discounts can prop up early sales, but they're costly and they end. Then the real, slower rate shows, and you've taught shoppers a lower price.

cards.title: Each stage pays for the next.
body: Maya maps the launch as steps, each with a clear test:
list: **Stage 1:** 40 cafés and health stores in one city. Do they reorder?
**Stage 2:** a regional chain, around 30 stores near those cafés. Do supermarket shoppers buy?
**Stage 3:** a national chain, with real sales-per-store numbers to show.
cards.callout: The proof from one stage is the pitch for the next.
cards.softwareNote: A new app often launches to one community first, then opens wider once people keep using it. Retention plays the role that reorders play for a drink.

cards.title: Going step by step has costs.
body: Sequencing is slower. A rival could take the shelf space first. And inside a larger company, a small start can look like failure next to yearly sales targets, so Maya needs to agree on the test for each stage with her bosses up front.
Early fans can also mislead. Café regulars may pay more and care more than supermarket shoppers. That's why stage 2 tests a new type of buyer, not just more of the same.

cards.title: Ten weeks in, the cafés keep reordering.
body: Cafés reorder every week. Health stores sell steadily but slower. The head of sales says the drink is proven and wants all 600 stores now.

options.text: Go national. The cafés prove it works
options.feedback: It skips a stage. Cafés show that ginger fans buy it, not that busy supermarket shoppers will pick it off a crowded shelf.

options.text: Pitch the regional chain for stores near the cafés, using the reorder data
options.feedback: **Launch sequencing** again: the next step tests the next type of buyer, near people who already know the drink, while the risk is still small.

options.text: Stay in cafés and add cafés in five more cities
options.feedback: Safe and likely to work, but it repeats a test already passed. The big unknown, supermarkets, stays unanswered.

cards.title: Win a small shelf before asking for a big one.
body: Two ideas did the work here. **Who to sell to first** pointed Maya to people who already buy drinks like hers. **Launch sequencing** turned their reorders into the case for each next stage.
**Try it today:** write down where your next product or service could start small, and the one number that would earn you the next stage.
